# Mathematical and notational reference {#sec-math-reference}

## Notation and dimensions

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $L$, $d$, $\mathcal H$ | Number of sites, local dimension, Hilbert space |
| $X,Y,Z$ or $\sigma^a$ | Pauli matrices, eigenvalues $\pm1$ |
| $S^a=\sigma^a/2$ | Spin one-half operators, eigenvalues $\pm1/2$ |
| $\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_{\bar A}\rho$ | Reduced state of region $A$ |
| $S$, $S_n$ | von Neumann and Rényi entropy, in nats |
| $\|O\|$, $\|O\|_1$, $\|O\|_2$ | Operator, trace, and Hilbert–Schmidt norms |
| $\langle O\rangle$, $\mathbb E X$, $\overline O$ | Quantum expectation, ensemble mean, stated time average |
| $D$, $v_B$, $v_E$ | Diffusion coefficient, butterfly velocity, entanglement velocity |
| $\mathcal L$, $\mathcal D[L]$ | Liouvillian generator, Lindblad dissipator |
| $\chi$, $\lambda$, $\theta$ | Bond dimension or susceptibility; rapidity/parameter and filling notation are defined locally |

Set $\hbar=k_B=1$. Energy has inverse-time units, momentum has inverse-length
units, and a diffusion coefficient has length squared per time. A lattice
constant is set to one when positions count sites. Check units before comparing
formulas written with Pauli and spin normalization.

## Singular values, Schmidt values, and norms

Every complex matrix has $M=U\Sigma V^\dagger$, with nonnegative singular
values $s_a$. The operator norm is $\max_as_a$, the trace norm is
$\sum_as_a$, and the Hilbert–Schmidt norm is $(\sum_as_a^2)^{1/2}$.
For a Hermitian matrix, the singular values are absolute eigenvalues.
$\|AB\|\leq\|A\|\|B\|$ and
$|\operatorname{Tr}A^\dagger B|\leq\|A\|_2\|B\|_2$ are useful
forms of submultiplicativity and Cauchy–Schwarz.

For a pure bipartite state, reshape coefficients into $M$. Then
$\rho_A=MM^\dagger$ and its eigenvalues are $s_a^2$. This derivation
explains why SVD is both an entanglement calculation and the optimal local
compression operation. Do not assume a tensor's singular values are physical
Schmidt values unless its environments represent orthonormal states.

## Fourier conventions and distributions

For a continuum function use
$f(k)=\int dx\,e^{-ikx}f(x)$ and
$f(x)=\int dk\,e^{ikx}f(k)/(2\pi)$. The derivative becomes $ik$.
For time use $f(\omega)=\int dt\,e^{i\omega t}f(t)$, so
$\partial_t\to-i\omega$. A retarded function vanishes for negative time
and is analytic for $\operatorname{Im}\omega>0$ with this convention.

The distribution identity
$1/(x+i0^+)=\mathcal P(1/x)-i\pi\delta(x)$ follows by writing
$1/(x+i\eta)=x/(x^2+\eta^2)-i\eta/(x^2+\eta^2)$ and taking
$\eta\to0^+$ under a smooth test-function integral. The second term
integrates to $-i\pi$ times the test function at zero. This identity controls
spectral and response signs; an unannounced opposite Fourier convention changes
them.

## Gaussian integrals and diffusion

The integral $\int dx\,e^{-a x^2}=\sqrt{\pi/a}$ for $a>0$ follows by
squaring it and changing to polar coordinates. Completing the square gives
$\int dk\,e^{-Dtk^2+ikx}/(2\pi)
=(4\pi Dt)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(4Dt)}$. Its variance is $2Dt$.
These formulas explain both a diffusion Green function and the low-momentum
Kibble–Zurek excitation integral; the physical mechanisms are different despite
the shared mathematics.

## Probability, conditioning, and nonlinear averages

A conditioned quantity $X(m)$ depends on an outcome or measurement record
$m$ drawn with probability $p_m$. The law of total expectation gives
$\mathbb E X=\sum_mp_m X(m)$. A density matrix averages linearly,
$\overline\rho=\sum_mp_m\rho_m$, but entropy does not:
$S(\overline\rho)\geq\sum_mp_m S(\rho_m)$ by concavity. For purity the
inequality is reversed under linear mixing because the squared norm is convex.

Jensen's inequality states $f(\mathbb E X)\leq\mathbb E f(X)$ for convex
$f$. Applying $f=-\ln$ gives
$-\ln\mathbb E p\leq\mathbb E[-\ln p]$ for positive $p$.
This separates annealed purity entropies from typical trajectory entropies. It
does not imply that an unnormalized trajectory ensemble can be averaged with
uniform weights; physical Born probabilities are required.

For independent samples, the mean's variance is $\operatorname{Var}(X)/N$.
For correlated samples $X_t$, it also includes covariances:
$\operatorname{Var}(\overline X)=N^{-2}\sum_{tt'}\operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_{t'})$.
The effective number of independent data points can be far smaller than the
number of stored times. Bootstrap the actual independent sampling units.

## Matrix exponentials and expansions

The series $e^A=\sum_nA^n/n!$ converges for every finite matrix. If $A$ and
$B$ commute, $e^{A+B}=e^Ae^B$; otherwise commutators appear. To leading
orders,
$\ln(e^Ae^B)=A+B+\tfrac12[A,B]+\cdots$. A symmetric product cancels
the leading even-in-step asymmetry and produces a second-order integrator.
An asymptotic many-body expansion may fail to converge uniformly with system
size even when every finite matrix exponential exists. Floquet expansions
require local estimates, not a naive smallness test on an extensive total norm.

## Scaling and asymptotic claims

A scaling form $C(x,t)=t^{-1/z}f(x/t^{1/z})$ specifies both an exponent and a
function, with possible amplitudes and corrections. Its conserved integral is
constant. A second moment scales as $t^{2/z}$ only if the scaling function's
second moment exists and tails outside the scaling regime do not dominate.
Finite-time effective exponents are logarithmic slopes, not automatically the
asymptotic exponent. A robust fit varies time and size windows and considers
plausible corrections.

The order of limits is mathematical content. A finite chain has recurrences;
a finite-dimensional Lindbladian can have a unique analytic steady state even
when a sequence of larger systems develops a transition. A prethermal regime
has a parametrically long lifetime but need not survive $t\to\infty$ at
fixed frequency. Write those limits before giving a phase label.

## Two useful worked checks

**Diffusion pole.** Fourier transforming
$\partial_tn=D\partial_x^2n$ gives
$(-i\omega+Dk^2)n=\text{source}$. The retarded pole is
$\omega=-iDk^2$ in the lower half plane, consistent with decay
$e^{-Dk^2t}$. A pole in the upper half plane would signal either instability or
a sign-convention error.

**A Bell-state partial transpose.** The partial transpose of
$|\Phi^+\rangle\langle\Phi^+|$ on the second qubit is
$\mathsf{Swap}/2$, with eigenvalues $1/2,1/2,1/2,-1/2$. Its trace norm is
2, giving logarithmic negativity $\ln2$. The classical correlated mixture has
no negative eigenvalue and zero negativity despite identical one-site entropies.
This is a compact demonstration of why mixed-state entropy alone cannot measure
entanglement.
